n: The Lord continues with a tour of wild animals. Does Job know when mountain goats give birth or watch over deer as they calve?

f.g: The ibex, a mountain goat of the Near East.

n: Can he count the months of their pregnancy or know their time to give birth?
They crouch, give birth, and are freed from labor pains — all without human help. God attends to births no human sees.

f.g: Deliver their young, ending their labor pains.

n: Their young grow strong in the open field, then leave and don’t come back.

f.g: Here the open field or grain.

n: Who set the wild donkey free and untied its ropes?

f.g: The onager, a wild donkey that can’t be tamed.

n: God gave it the wilderness for a home and salt flats for its dwelling.
It laughs at the noise of the city and never hears a driver’s shouts. It is free in a way no domesticated animal is.

f.g: A taskmaster who drives working animals.

n: It roams the mountains for pasture, searching for anything green.
Will the wild ox agree to serve Job or spend the night by his feeding trough?

f.g: Hebrew re’em — the wild ox (aurochs), a huge and powerful animal, not a mythical horse.

n: Can Job tie it with a rope to plow a furrow, or make it harrow the valleys behind him?
Will he trust it because it’s strong, and leave his heavy work to it?

f.w: wilt thou leave thy labour to him?
f.g: Will you rely on it to do your farm work?

n: Can he count on it to bring in his grain and gather it to his threshing floor?
The ostrich flaps its wings proudly, but they aren’t like the stork’s feathers — it can’t fly.

f.g: Possibly “the stork,” a bird known for caring for its young.

n: She leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the sand.

f.g: Ostriches lay eggs in shallow pits in the sand.

n: She forgets that a foot could crush them or a wild animal trample them.

f.w: the wild beast may break them

n: She treats her young harshly, as if they weren’t hers, and doesn’t worry that her labor might be wasted.
God didn’t give her wisdom or a share of understanding. God made creatures with odd, even comical traits — and delights in them anyway.

f.w: God hath deprived her of wisdom
f.g: An affectionate, humorous description of the ostrich’s apparent carelessness.

n: Yet when she spreads her wings to run, she laughs at horse and rider — she can outrun them.

f.w: she scorneth the horse and his rider
f.g: Ostriches can run very fast, about 40 miles per hour.

n: Did Job give the war horse its strength or clothe its neck with a flowing mane?

f.g: Probably “with a mane” — the Hebrew word suggests quivering or rippling.

n: Can Job make it leap like a locust? Its proud snorting is terrifying.

f.g: As a locust — leaping and bounding.

n: It paws the valley floor, delights in its strength, and charges into the battle line.

f.w: goeth on to meet the armed men

n: It laughs at fear, is never frightened, and doesn’t turn back from the sword.
Arrows rattle in the quiver against its side, along with flashing spear and javelin.
Trembling with excitement, it devours the ground and can’t stand still when the trumpet sounds.
At the trumpet blast it snorts “Aha!” and smells the battle from far off, with commanders shouting.
Does the hawk soar by Job’s wisdom and spread its wings toward the south in migration?

f.w: stretch her wings toward the south
f.g: Migrate — many birds of prey pass through the Near East each year.

n: Does the eagle rise at Job’s command and build its nest high up?

f.g: Possibly the griffon vulture, which nests on high cliffs.

n: It lives on cliffs, resting on rocky crags and strongholds.
From there it scans for food; its eyes spot prey from far away.

f.g: Birds of prey have remarkably keen vision.

n: Its young feed on blood, and wherever the dead lie, it is there. Even harsh parts of nature are under God’s care and design.

f.w: where the slain are, there is she
